extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mathematics and philosophy interested in constructive/intuitionistic mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize the standards, principles, and proof-requirements that characterize constructive (intuitionistic, recursive, Bishop-style, and type-theoretic) approaches to mathematics; explain what constructive proofs must provide and which axioms/principles are accepted or rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: BHK-interpretations of logical connectives and quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The meanings of logical connectives and quantifiers are given algorithmically: to prove P ∨ Q you must have a proof of P or a proof of Q; to prove P ∧ Q you must have proofs of both P and Q; a proof of P → Q is an algorithm transforming any proof of P into a proof of Q; to prove ¬P show that P implies a contradiction; to prove ∃x P(x) construct an object x and prove P(x); to prove ∀x∈S P(x) give an algorithm which, given x and data witnessing x∈S, produces a proof of P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Brouwer–Heyting–Kolmogorov (BHK) interpretations are the constructive standard; they can be formalized via Kleene realizability. The entry repeatedly treats these as the criteria that distinguish constructive from classical proofs (i.e., classical uses of ¬¬, idealistic ∃, or the LEM are not permitted unless accompanied by constructive witnesses/algorithms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive treatment of negation and double negation
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove ¬p one may assume p and derive a contradiction (this is constructive); but assuming ¬p and deriving a contradiction only yields ¬¬p, and from ¬¬p one cannot in general conclude p constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes acceptable reductio-style proofs (deriving a contradiction from p is a constructive proof of ¬p) from nonconstructive uses of double negation-elimination. The entry gives examples (e.g., 'boojum' reasoning) to show that ¬¬∃x P(x) does not provide a constructive witness for ∃x P(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive proof requirement for disjunction/decidability (example: x=0 or x≠0)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive assertion 'for each real x, either x = 0 or x ≠ 0' requires an algorithm which, given a representation of a real x (and the data that x is real), decides which disjunct holds (outputs e.g. 0 for x=0 and 1 for x≠0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical obstacles (e.g., underflow and finite rational approximations) mean such decision procedures often do not exist; the SEP uses this as motivation for rejecting some classical principles under computational interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive proof requirements for least upper bounds (suprema)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'every nonempty S⊆ℝ that is bounded above has a least upper bound' constructively requires an algorithm which, given S, a member s∈S, and an upper bound for S, computes an object b and (1) shows b is a real number; (2) shows x ≤ b for each x∈S; and (3) given any b' < b, computes x∈S with x > b'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop's constructive theory weakens the classical statement: S has a least upper bound iff it is upper-order located (for α<β either β is an upper bound or ∃x∈S with x>α). This gives a precise constructive criterion (upper-order locatedness) that is necessary for a constructive supremum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive Intermediate Value Theorems (exact and approximate forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact-root version: to prove 'if f continuous on [0,1] with f(0)·f(1) < 0 then ∃x∈(0,1) with f(x)=0' one must provide an algorithm which, given f, a modulus of continuity for f, and f(0), f(1), computes x (a real) and proves f(x)=0. Approximate/ε-version: to prove 'for each ε>0 ∃x∈(0,1) with |f(x)|<ε' requires an algorithm which, given f, a modulus of continuity, f(0), f(1), and ε, computes such an x and verifies the bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exact version is nonconstructive in general (entails LLPO); a weaker approximate form can be proved constructively (using interval-halving or approximate-interval-halving). A stronger constructive IVT that suffices in practice assumes local nonzeroness and yields an exact root constructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited Principle of Omniscience (LPO), Lesser LPO (LLPO), and Markov's Principle (MP)
rubrics_metrics.description: LPO: for each binary sequence (a_n) either all a_n=0 or ∃n with a_n=1. LLPO: for sequences with at most one 1, either all even terms are 0 or all odd terms are 0. MP: if it is contradictory that all a_n=0 then ∃n with a_n=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LPO and LLPO are generally nonconstructive (false under recursive interpretations and refutable in Kripke models); MP is weaker, represents unbounded search, and is controversial (viewed with suspicion by many constructive mathematicians) though consistent with some constructive frameworks. The entry uses these principles to classify constructive vs nonconstructive theorems (e.g., which IVT versions imply which principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous choice principles (CC1 and CC2)
rubrics_metrics.description: CC1: Any function from ℕ^ℕ to ℕ is continuous. CC2: If P ⊆ ℕ^ℕ × ℕ and ∀α ∈ ℕ^ℕ ∃n with (α,n)∈P, then there is a function f:ℕ^ℕ→ℕ with (α,f(α))∈P for all α (i.e., a continuous choice function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwerian acceptance of CC1–CC2 enforces strong continuity properties (e.g., every mapping from ℝ to ℝ is pointwise continuous) and refutes omniscience principles like LPO/LLPO; these are foundational constraints one must accept/verify when working in that intuitionistic setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan theorem for detachable bars (FT_D) and notions of fan/bar/uniform bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: a detachable subset σ of ℕ^* is a fan if closed under restrictions and every node has finitely many immediate extensions; B⊆σ is a bar if every infinite path is blocked by B; B is uniform if there is n such that every path of length n is blocked. FT_D: every detachable bar of a fan is uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FT_D is a key intuitionistic principle (its classical contrapositive is König's Lemma). Acceptance of fan theorems influences compactness and continuity results (e.g., Brouwer's uniform continuity theorem). The entry explains where detachability matters and how weaker/stronger fan theorems relate to classical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform continuity theorem (Brouwerian consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Brouwerian hypotheses (continuous choice CC1–CC2 together with a form of the fan theorem), every mapping from a compact (complete, totally bounded) metric space into a metric space is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a major constructive conclusion that contrasts with some classical theorems; it must be read inside the intuitionistic framework where 'function' and 'real number' are given constructive meanings. Use of this theorem as a correctness/acceptability criterion requires checking the underlying constructive hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom CPF (computable partial functions) in recursive constructive mathematics (RUSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: CPF: there is an enumeration φ_0, φ_1, ... of all partial functions ℕ→ℕ with countable domains. RUSS takes objects/procedures to be given by Gödel-numberings and all procedures to be recursive, and uses intuitionistic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CPF (and the recursive stance) yields many recursive counterexamples to classical theorems (Specker sequences, ε-singular covers of ℝ, pointwise but not uniformly continuous functions, etc.). When evaluating work in the RUSS paradigm, the recursive/numbering axioms and their consequences are the standard constraints to check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bishop-style constructive mathematics (BISH) methodological criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: BISH practices mathematics using intuitionistic logic with an emphasis on algorithmic content but without fixing a single primitive notion of 'algorithm' (i.e., proofs should be algorithmically interpretable and readable as analysis). BISH results are intended to be interpretable in multiple models (intuitionistic, recursive, classical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criterion for constructive work: restrict to intuitionistic logic and present proofs so they supply the algorithmic information required by the BHK-interpretation. Bishop's approach emphasizes readability and multiple interpretability rather than formal logical pinning-down; evaluate proofs for explicit constructive content (witnesses, moduli, algorithms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predeterminate (lawlike) vs free-choice sequences and continuity/choice consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive accounts of sequences may be predeterminate (given by a rule) or free-choice (terms constructed successively). Brouwer's admission of free-choice sequences motivates strong continuity and choice principles (continuous choice, fan theorems) and affects which classical theorems hold constructively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing constructive arguments, be explicit about what kind of sequences are permitted; many strong constructive principles (and resulting continuity statements) depend on admitting free-choice sequences and attendant continuity/choice axioms.
